--- title: Nearest neighbors description: Find approximate nearest neighbors with NNDescent, and run UMAP on a precomputed graph. jupyter: python3 bread-crumbs: false --- The first thing UMAP does is find every point's nearest neighbors. polars-umap exposes that step on its own: a Rust port of [PyNNDescent](https://github.com/lmcinnes/pynndescent), the approximate nearest neighbor search that umap-learn uses. ## Finding neighbors ::: {#a052710f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars_umap as pu nn = digits.with_columns(nn=pl.col("pixels").umap.knn(k=5, random_state=0)) nn.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 3)
pixelsdigitnn
array[f64, 64]i64struct[2]
[0.0, 0.0, … 0.0]0{[0, 877, … 1167],[0.0, 10.954452, … 13.2665]}
[0.0, 0.0, … 0.0]1{[1, 93, … 1050],[0.0, 14.247807, … 19.672316]}
[0.0, 0.0, … 0.0]2{[2, 57, … 115],[0.0, 17.435596, … 25.942244]}
``` ::: ::: The result is a struct with two fields, both sorted by increasing distance: - `indices`: an `Array(UInt32, k)` of row numbers; - `distances`: an `Array(Float32, k)` of distances in the chosen `metric`. As in PyNNDescent, every row counts as its own nearest neighbor: it's usually first, at distance 0. Ask for `k=6` to get five other rows. Because the indices are row numbers, you can join information about the neighbors back in. For example, how often is a neighbor the same digit? ::: {#3b17ce2f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( nn.with_row_index("row") .select("row", "digit", neighbor=pl.col("nn").struct.field("indices").arr.to_list()) .explode("neighbor") .filter(pl.col("neighbor") != pl.col("row")) .join( digits.with_row_index("neighbor").select("neighbor", neighbor_digit="digit"), on="neighbor", ) .select(same_digit=(pl.col("digit") == pl.col("neighbor_digit")).mean()) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (1, 1)
same_digit
f64
0.981914
``` ::: ::: ## How approximate? NNDescent trades a little accuracy for a lot of speed. Compared with an exact search: ::: {#2ff2e270 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors k = 10 approx = np.asarray( digits.select(pl.col("pixels").umap.knn(k=k, random_state=0).struct.field("indices")) .to_series() .to_list() ) exact = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X).kneighbors(X, return_distance=False) recall = np.mean([len(set(a) & set(e)) / k for a, e in zip(approx, exact)]) f"recall@{k}: {recall:.1%}" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 'recall@10: 99.6%' ``` ::: ::: When there are fewer rows than `k`, the search is exact and the missing neighbors are null. ## UMAP on a precomputed graph If you already have neighbors, for example from an exact search, a vector database or FAISS, pass them to `umap_from_knn()` and UMAP skips its own search. The original vectors aren't needed: ::: {#74f7bb7a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} dist, idx = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=15).fit(X).kneighbors(X) graph = pl.DataFrame({"indices": idx, "distances": dist.astype(np.float32)}) graph.select(xy=pu.umap_from_knn("indices", "distances", random_state=0)).head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 1)
xy
array[f32, 2]
[-4.64634, -1.344931]
[5.53124, 2.986445]
[7.111255, 2.451521]
``` ::: ::: The graph can include each row itself (usually first, at distance 0) or leave it out. Every row needs the same number of neighbors. `init="pca"` isn't available here, because it needs the vectors.
